sections.title: Origin of life: the Oparin–Haldane theory and the Miller–Urey experiment
Evidences of evolution: morphological, anatomical, palaeontological, embryological and biochemical
Human evolution from Ramapithecus to modern man

summary: Life arose by chemical evolution (Oparin 1924, Haldane 1929) in a reducing atmosphere of CH₄, NH₃, H₂ and water vapour with no free O₂, energised by UV and lightning: monomers → polymers → coacervates/microspheres → protocell → anaerobic heterotroph.
Miller–Urey (1953) sparked CH₄, NH₃, H₂ (2 : 2 : 1) and steam for a week and obtained amino acids (glycine, alanine) — monomers, not life.
Homologous organs (same origin, different use) show divergent evolution; analogous organs (different origin, same use) show convergent evolution; vestigial organs and atavism point to ancestors.
Connecting links — Peripatus, Neopilina, Balanoglossus, lungfish, Archaeopteryx, platypus — and the horse series (Eohippus → Equus, toes 4 → 1) are the classic fossil and living evidence.
Haeckel's biogenetic law (embryos), Nuttall's precipitin test, cytochrome c and the universal genetic code (biochemistry) complete the evidence.
Lamarck (1809): use and disuse + inheritance of acquired characters — refuted by Weismann (22 generations of tailed mice; germplasm theory).
Darwin (1859): overproduction, struggle, variation, natural selection ("survival of the fittest", Spencer); weakness — no theory of variation or heredity. De Vries: mutation, Oenothera.
Neo-Darwinism: mutation + recombination + selection + isolation (+ drift, gene flow); the population evolves; Hardy–Weinberg p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1; Biston betularia is directional selection.

units.title: Animal Diversity and Classification
topics: Diagnostic features and classification of animals from Protozoa to Chordata

sections.title: Diagnostic features and classification of animals from Protozoa to Chordata

summary: Animals are classified by level of organisation, symmetry, germ layers, coelom and segmentation: cellular → Porifera; tissue, radial, diploblastic → Coelenterata; acoelomate → Platyhelminthes; pseudocoelomate → Aschelminthes; schizocoelous protostomes → Annelida, Arthropoda, Mollusca; enterocoelous deuterostomes → Echinodermata, Hemichord
Protozoa are grouped by locomotion: pseudopodia (Amoeba, Entamoeba), flagella (Euglena, Trypanosoma, Leishmania), none (Sporozoa: Plasmodium), cilia (Paramecium, Balantidium).
Porifera: ostia, osculum, canal system, choanocytes, spicules or spongin, gemmules; Calcarea, Hexactinellida (Euplectella), Demospongiae (Euspongia, Spongilla).
Coelenterata: radial, diploblastic, coelenteron, nematocysts, polyp and medusa, metagenesis in Obelia; Hydrozoa, Scyphozoa, Anthozoa.
Platyhelminthes (flame cells; Fasciola, Taenia) and Aschelminthes (pseudocoel, complete gut, separate sexes; Ascaris, Wuchereria, Ancylostoma, Enterobius).
Annelida: metameres, setae/parapodia, closed circulation, nephridia; Polychaeta (Nereis), Oligochaeta (Pheretima), Hirudinea (Hirudinaria).

Arthropoda, the largest phylum: jointed legs, chitin, haemocoel, open circulation; Crustacea (2 pairs of antennae, gills, green glands), Myriapoda, Insecta (3 pairs of legs, tracheae, Malpighian tubules), Arachnida (4 pairs of legs, book lungs, no antennae).
Mollusca: mantle, shell, radula, ctenidia; seven classes from Neopilina to Sepia; Echinodermata: pentaradial adults, water vascular system, tube feet; Asteroidea to Crinoidea.

units.title: Animal Tissues and Histology
topics: Epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous tissues: structure, location and function

sections.title: Epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous tissues: structure, location and function

summary: A tissue is a group of similar cells with a common origin and function; the four primary tissues are epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous.

Epithelium rests on a basement membrane, has almost no matrix, is avascular and arises from all three germ layers; it is named by layers and cell shape — squamous (alveoli, capillaries), cuboidal (kidney tubules, thyroid), columnar (stomach, intestine), ciliated (oviduct), pseudostratified (trachea), stratified squamous (skin, oesophagus)
Glands are exocrine, endocrine or heterocrine (pancreas), and secrete in merocrine (salivary), apocrine (mammary) or holocrine (sebaceous) fashion.

Connective tissue has few cells (fibroblasts, macrophages, mast cells, plasma cells, fat cells) in abundant matrix with collagen, elastic and reticular fibres: areolar, adipose, tendon, ligament, cartilage, bone, blood and lymph.

Cartilage is avascular with chondrin matrix — hyaline (joints, trachea), elastic (pinna, epiglottis), fibrocartilage (intervertebral discs); bone has ossein and hydroxyapatite, osteocytes in lacunae and Haversian systems.
Blood: 55 % plasma; RBCs (5 million/mm³, 120 days, no nucleus), WBCs (6000–8000/mm³; neutrophils most, basophils fewest, monocytes largest) and platelets (clotting).

Muscle: skeletal (striated, voluntary, multinucleate), smooth (spindle, involuntary) and cardiac (branched, intercalated discs, myogenic); in contraction actin slides over myosin, the A band stays constant and the I band and H zone shorten.

Nervous tissue: neurons (cyton with Nissl granules, dendrites, axon, myelin from Schwann cells or oligodendrocytes, nodes of Ranvier) and neuroglia (astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, Schwann cells, microglia, ependymal cells).

sections.title: Plasmodium: habitat, structure, life cycle and types of malaria
Earthworm (Pheretima): morphology, body systems, physiology and economic importance
Frog (Rana): morphology, body systems and physiology

summary: Plasmodium (Sporozoa) is a digenetic intracellular parasite: asexual schizogony in man (intermediate host) — liver cells, then the 48-hour Golgi cycle in RBCs — and sexual phase in the female Anopheles (definitive host) — gametes, zygote, ookinete, oocyst, sporozoites in the salivary glands.
The sporozoite infects man and the gametocyte infects the mosquito; the zygote is the only diploid stage; the fever follows the synchronous bursting of RBCs and the release of haemozoin.
P. vivax (benign tertian, relapses from hypnozoites, commonest in Nepal), P. falciparum (malignant tertian, cerebral malaria), P. malariae (quartan, 72 h) and P. ovale (ovale tertian).
Pheretima posthuma: about 100–120 segments; prostomium; clitellum 14–16; perichaetine setae; female pore 14, male pores 18, papillae 17 and 19, spermathecal pores 5/6–8/9.

Earthworm gut: pharynx 4, gizzard 8–9, stomach 9–14 with calciferous glands, caeca and typhlosole from 26; closed circulation with Hb in plasma and four pairs of hearts (7, 9, 12, 13); cutaneous respiration; septal, integumentary and pharyngeal nephridia.

The earthworm is a protandrous hermaphrodite: testes 10–11, ovaries 13, spermathecae 6–9; cross-fertilisation, fertilisation in the cocoon, direct development; it is the farmer's friend and the basis of vermicomposting.

The frog (Rana tigrina) breathes by skin, buccopharynx and lungs (buccal force pump); its three-chambered heart with sinus venosus and spiral valve gives a double but incomplete circulation; RBCs are nucleated.

The frog is ureotelic with mesonephric kidneys; the male's ureter is a urinogenital duct; it has 10 pairs of cranial nerves, 9 vertebrae and a urostyle; fertilisation is external after amplexus, and thyroxine drives metamorphosis of the tadpole.
